The early life stages of Japanese seabass (Lateolabrax japonicus) are characterized by a brief embryonic period when temperatures are elevated. At a water temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C], an extremely rapid developmental program unfolds, with hatching occurring after only 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days]. This short incubation time is typical for temperate perciform fishes spawning in warm coastal waters during late spring. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae carry a substantial endogenous nutritional reserve; their wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 1.4 millimeters. The mass of the freshly hatched prolarva reflects the considerable yolk investment allocated by the female. Following eclosion, these endotrophic larvae remain entirely dependent on their yolk reserves for nourishment while undergoing rapid early differentiation. The mouth remains closed during this lecithotrophic phase, and the larvae drift as part of the ichthyoplankton assemblage, gradually exhausting their endogenous supply before the critical transition to exogenous feeding must occur.

Females of this species attain sexual maturity upon reaching a specific body size, a pattern common among iteroparous marine teleosts. Field surveys and histological examinations of ovarian tissue indicate that puberty is triggered when individuals reach a total length at puberty of 50 centimeters [Lp = 50 centimeters]. This threshold appears to be closely tied to the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic demands of vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning activity. Individuals below this length are rarely observed with developing oocytes, suggesting a strong size-based gating mechanism for reproductive activation. The onset of gonadal recrudescence typically occurs in late autumn, with females preparing for the spring spawning season. Achieving this size requires several years of somatic growth, and variability in local prey availability can significantly influence the age at which this length benchmark is attained. The consistency of this observation across multiple populations in Japanese coastal waters underscores the robust nature of 50 centimeters as a reliable indicator of reproductive readiness in this commercially valuable species.

Reproductive output in Japanese seabass is remarkable for its scale, with females exhibiting exceptionally high fecundity during the spawning season. Individual females produce between 1,726,242 and 17,822,576 eggs per spawning season [Ri = between 1,726,242 and 17,822,576 eggs per spawning season]. This extraordinary fecundity is characteristic of pelagic spawners that produce small, buoyant eggs subject to high mortality rates during the planktonic larval phase. Such a life-history strategy, emphasizing high numerical output over per-offspring investment, is typical of many coastal perciform fishes that broadcast their gametes into the water column. The batch fecundity is positively correlated with female body size, with larger, older gravid fish contributing disproportionately to the annual egg production of the population. This high reproductive potential, however, is counterbalanced by intense density-dependent mortality during the early larval stages, meaning that only a tiny fraction of the spawned eggs ultimately survive to the juvenile stage under natural conditions.

Adult Japanese seabass are capable of reaching considerable sizes, with the ultimate total length recorded for the species being 102 centimeters [Li = 102 centimeters]. This maximum size represents the asymptotic length approached by the oldest and most successful individuals in the population, a figure established through long-term mark-recapture studies and commercial fishery catch data. Individuals approaching this upper size limit are rare and typically represent females, which exhibit greater longevity and faster growth rates than males after the onset of maturity. The species displays indeterminate growth, a trait common among teleosts, allowing continued, though decelerating, somatic expansion throughout adult life. The largest specimens are usually found in less exploited, deeper offshore waters of the East China Sea, suggesting that habitat quality and reduced fishing pressure facilitate the expression of this full growth potential. Reaching a length of 102 centimeters requires several decades, a fact that makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing of its largest size classes.

Longevity records for Japanese seabass indicate a maximum lifespan that may be significantly underestimated by current sampling methods. The oldest individuals recovered from wild populations, based on otolith annulus readings, have been aged at 38 years, but this figure probably underestimates the true maximum lifespan, which is projected to be approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years]. This discrepancy likely arises from the selective removal of older fish by commercial fisheries, which preferentially target the largest and most fecund individuals. The species exhibits a classic pattern of slow growth and late maturation typical of a K-selected marine fish, where investment in somatic tissue is balanced against the energetic demands of repeated annual spawning events over a long reproductive lifespan. Understanding this extended natural longevity is critical for fisheries management, as the removal of older age classes can truncate the age structure and reduce the reproductive resilience of the population. The presence of very old individuals in the population contributes substantially to the overall spawning stock biomass and ensures multiple breeding opportunities across a lifetime.
